text.en: Asha wanted to find the height of a tall tree without climbing it. "Use the angle of elevation," said her teacher.

Trigonometric identities hold for angles for which both sides are defined: sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1, 1 + tan^2 A = sec^2 A and 1 + cot^2 A = cosec^2 A. They help to simplify expressions and to prove other relations.
In heights and distances, the line of sight is the line from the eye to the object. The angle of elevation is the angle above the horizontal when we look up, and the angle of depression is the angle below it when we look down. For the same line of sight between two levels, the angle of elevation from below equals the angle of depression from above, by alternate interior angles.
To solve such problems, draw a neat figure, mark the right-angled triangles and use tan, sin or cos as needed. Problems may involve one angle of elevation or depression, or both together.

A trigonometric identity is true for every angle for which both sides are defined. Three examples are sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, one plus tangent squared equals secant squared, and one plus cotangent squared equals cosecant squared.

text.en: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. It is the longest side, and its name does not depend on which acute angle you choose.

board.text: Locate the hypotenuse first

text.en: Point to the chosen angle. The opposite side does not touch it. The adjacent leg touches it and is the shorter side that is not the hypotenuse.

board.text: Opposite and adjacent depend on the angle

text.en: In a three-four-five triangle with opposite side three, sine is three fifths.

board.text: sin A = opposite / hypotenuse

text.en: If the adjacent side is four in that triangle, cosine is four fifths.

board.text: cos A = adjacent / hypotenuse

text.en: For the same angle, tangent is three fourths. The hypotenuse is not part of this ratio.

board.text: tan A = opposite / adjacent

text.en: If all three side lengths double, their side ratios stay the same. That is why a trigonometric ratio depends on the angle rather than on triangle size.

text.en: Secant is one over cosine, cosecant is one over sine, and cotangent is one over tangent wherever the reciprocal is defined.

text.en: The two shorter squares add to the hypotenuse squared. Divide through by the last square to get sine squared plus cosine squared equals one.

text.en: From sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, divide every term by cosine squared. This gives tangent squared plus one equals secant squared.

text.en: This time divide every term of the first identity by sine squared. The result is one plus cotangent squared equals cosecant squared.

text.en: The square of cosine is one minus nine twenty-fifths, or sixteen twenty-fifths. Cosine is positive for an acute angle, so it equals four fifths.

problem.en: From a point 10 m from a tower the angle of elevation is 45 degrees. Find the height.

text.en: tan 45 = height / 10.
The height is 10 m.

problem.en: If sin A = 5/13 and A is acute, find cos A and tan A.

why.en: Cosine is positive for an acute angle, so cos A = 12/13.

text.en: Divide sin A by cos A to get tan A = 5/12.

why.en: The denominators cancel in the ratio.

problem.en: A student’s eyes are 1.5 m above level ground and 10 m from the base of a pole. The angle of elevation to the top is 45°. Find the pole height.

text.en: Rise above eye level = 10 × tan 45° = 10 m.

why.en: Tangent relates the vertical difference to the horizontal distance.

text.en: Total height = 10 m + 1.5 m = 11.5 m.

why.en: The pole also extends below the horizontal through the student’s eyes.

problem.en: A balcony is 8 m above level ground. A marker lies on the ground and the angle of depression is 45°. Find its horizontal distance from the wall.

text.en: Use the matching elevation angle at the marker.

why.en: The two horizontal lines are parallel, so this angle is 45°.

text.en: tan 45° = 8/d = 1, so d = 8 m.

why.en: At 45° the two legs of the right triangle are equal.
